newsitem.title: TURKEY: Privatisation plans to boost Turkish bourse in 97.
newsitem.headline: Privatisation plans to boost Turkish bourse in 97.

text.p: Turkish brokers see privatisation pumping cash and morale into the Istanbul stock market next year as planned sell-offs become a major hope for Turkey's economic problems.
"It is hard for privatisation to be realised in the short-term, but the market will buy on expectations," said Irfan Sakin, assistant general manager at Global securities.
"The goverment has got to find revenue to tackle economic problems and it has got a sufficient majority in Parliament," he added.
Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan aims to complete sell-offs worth $15 billion through privatisation and the leasing of power plants.
Since 1986, Turkey has raised only $3 billion from privatisation due to political turmoil, legal barriers and court annulments and a lack of consensus across the economic community.

"Hope lies in privatisation together with tax revenues," said Nalan Erkarakas, assistant general manager at Kentbank. "Budget and trade deficits have been serious problems and state borrowing has expanded."

The government has targeted a zero-deficit budget for 1997 after an expected 1,300 trillion lira ($12.6 billion) deficit this year. Next year's draft budget aims to collect 6,255 trillion lira in revenue -- 70 percent from taxes and the rest from non-tax items led by sell-offs.
Berra Kilic, assistant general manager at Ata securities, said progress on privatisation was expected.
"If five or six big sell-offs could be achieved towards the end of 1997, then the (treasury) balance will change," she said.
In the short-term, bourse activity in December might also be boosted by end-1996 company profit prospects, brokers said.
"We may have a end-year (upwards) movement on balance sheets this year, in contrast to recent years, because the mood is suitable," Kilic said.
In dollar terms, the stock market index stood at $0.88 on Wednesday, compared to a $1 record on April 8 and $0.67 at the end of last year. Analysts say the target by end-1996 is $1.
Brokers also said the stock market was supported by the strict joint control of the Treasury and central bank over currency and money markets.

"The markets are confident that foreign currencies will move under the central bank's supervision, but there is some caution arising from the Treasury's domestic debt policy, which is variable," said Kilic.
"The tendency to keep interest rates artificially low without a decrease in the government's domestic borrowing need is irritating all the markets," she added.
Government officials have said the zero-deficit 1997 budget would lead to a reduction in domestic borrowing and high real interest rates of around 20 percent.
Turkey's domestic debt surged to 2,891 trillion lira at end-October from 1,361 trillion at the end of 1995. Year-on-year wholesale inflation stood at 85.7 percent in November.
